food.text: The Afanasievo culture, which spread across the Altai Mountains and into Mongolia between about 3300 and 2500 BCE, is considered the earliest herding culture of East Asia. Their rise brought the first domesticated sheep, goats and cattle into Inner Asia, marking the earliest spread of Near Eastern farm animals into the region.

Lipid residues preserved in pottery from the Botai culture of northern Kazakhstan show that people were drinking mare's milk as early as 3500 to 3700 BCE, providing compelling evidence of early dairy consumption.

Between 5500 and 3500 BCE, the Kelteminar people lived in the deserts of what are now Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. They fished, hunted and gathered along the Amu Darya and Zeravshan rivers, and gradually took up stockbreeding as well.

Around 3700 to 3300 BCE, people migrated across the Eurasian steppe from the Volga-Ural region and became the Afanasievo culture of the Altai Mountains. They brought domesticated sheep, goats and cattle with them, making them the earliest herders of East Asia.

Between 4000 and 3000 BCE, the Bolshemys people of the Altai Mountains in South Siberia lived as foot hunters. They pursued hoofed animals such as roe deer, musk deer, red deer, Siberian ibex and mouflon for food.

The Botai settlement in northern Kazakhstan, dated to about 3700 to 3100 BCE, had at least 153 pit-houses. Pottery excavated there contained traces of mare's milk, pointing to horse milking as part of daily life.

Kelteminar communities cooked their food in clay vessels shaped without the use of a potter's wheel. Whole tribal groups of around 100 to 120 people shared single huge houses measuring as much as 24 by 17 metres.

Afanasievo herding spread as far as Shatar Chuluu in central Mongolia, roughly 1,500 kilometres beyond the Altai Mountains. This expansion helped establish the long tradition of pastoralism that later defined life on the Mongolian steppe.

Migrating groups brought the bow and arrow and the dog into Kelteminar territory from the Hissar region between 6000 and 4000 BCE. These tools helped the Kelteminar people hunt more effectively alongside their fishing.

Despite their early mare's milk drinking, the horses kept by the Botai people were mostly ancestors of today's wild Przewalski's horse. They contributed only about 2.7 percent of the ancestry of modern domestic horses.

art.text: The Botai culture, who lived in what is now northern Kazakhstan around 3700 to 3100 BCE, made simple grey pottery decorated with geometric patterns. Their potters left the vessels unglazed, relying purely on carved and pressed designs for decoration.

The Afanasievo culture, which spread across south Siberia and into the Altai Mountains from around 3700 to 3300 BCE, produced painted pottery that resembles work from the much earlier Banpo culture of Neolithic China, dated to about 4000 BCE. Researchers see this as a sign of far-reaching cultural contact stretching from the Middle Yenisei region toward the Far East.

The Bolshemys culture, foot hunters active in the Altai mountains of south Siberia between 4000 and 3000 BCE, shaped thin-walled ceramic vessels with pointed or beet-shaped bottoms. Their pottery was heavily decorated with jagged lines, comb patterns, and zig-zag designs.

The Kelteminar culture of the Karakum and Kyzyl Kum deserts, active from about 5500 to 3500 BCE, built huge shared houses roughly 24 by 17 meters and up to 10 meters high. A single such house could shelter an entire community of about 100 to 120 people.

Botai potters filled their geometric pottery with specific motifs, including hatched triangles, rhombi, and step motifs. These recurring designs appear across the culture's known sites in northern Kazakhstan.

The main Botai settlement sat beside the Imanburlyq River, a tributary of the Ishim, and contained at least 153 pit-houses. Such a large cluster of dwellings points to a substantial community of builders in the region.

Afanasievo burials also held crafted objects of copper, bronze, gold, and silver, including awls and knives. These finds show the culture introducing early metalworking crafts to the region alongside its painted pottery traditions.

Kelteminar people adorned themselves with beads made from shells and manufactured stone axes as part of their craft work. These items came from communities spread across the deserts and river deltas of what are now Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.

Bolshemys people made thin-walled ceramic vessels with pointed or beet-shaped bottoms, later replaced by thicker vessels with round or flattened bottoms, decorated with jagged lines and comb patterns. This style closely resembles pottery of the Kelteminar culture of Central Asia and the Afanasevo culture of the Altai.

Beyond triangles and rhombi, Botai potters also pressed punctates, small dot-like marks, and circles into their grey, unglazed vessels. These extra motifs added variety to the culture's otherwise simple geometric pottery designs.

In rare cases, Bolshemys vessels carried print-comb ornamentation, a style more typical of the Chalcolithic art of the Eastern Urals and Tumen-Ob region. This detail shows how far pottery-decorating ideas could travel across the Siberian steppe.

war.text: In the Botai culture of what is now northern Kazakhstan, dated to about 3700 to 3100 BC, people hunted the wild horse species Equus ferus using bows, arrows, and spears. Researchers once believed nearly all of the horse remains found at Botai sites came from these hunted wild animals rather than tamed ones.

Kelteminar fishing communities living across the deserts and river deltas of what are now Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan between about 5500 and 3500 BCE gained the bow and arrow when Mesolithic groups moved in from the Hissar region between 6000 and 4000 BCE. These newcomers also brought the dog, part of a broader shift in hunting technology.

In the Bolshemys culture of the Altai Mountains in south Siberia, an Eneolithic culture dated to about 4000 to 3000 BC, the number of bifaces and arrowheads found at sites is five to ten times greater than in earlier Neolithic layers. These foot hunters used such weapons to hunt hoofed animals including roe deer, red deer, and Siberian ibex.

Near the village of Ust-Belaya, at the confluence of the Anadyr and Belaya Rivers in what is now Chukotka in far eastern Siberia, archaeologists found a toggled harpoon head in a grave. It shows that a walrus-hunting economy was active in the area around 3000 BCE.

This weapon-rich Eneolithic evidence comes from about 50 known Bolshemys culture monuments in the Altai foothills, along rivers including the Katun, Biya, Irtysh, and Ob, discovered in the 1970s by researcher B.H. Kadikov. Only one cemetery, called Large Cape, has been found there so far.

In the 1950s, archaeologist N.N. Dikov identified a burial site near Ust-Belaya belonging to a previously unknown people, who have been named after the village as the Ust-Belayan culture. Near the village, at the eastern end of the settlement, an ancient cemetery was partially destroyed during the construction of some warehouses.

science.text: The Botai culture flourished around 3700 to 3100 BC in what is now northern Kazakhstan, where people lived in settlements with at least 153 pit-houses along the Imanburlyq river. Pottery and horse-bone evidence there suggests the Botai people were domesticating and using horses on a large scale.

The Kelteminar culture (5500 to 3500 BCE) consisted of hunter-gatherer-fishermen living in the deserts of the Karakum and Kyzyl Kum and the river deltas of the Amu Darya and Zeravshan, in what are now Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan. Although they relied mainly on hunting, gathering and fishing, over time they also adopted stockbreeding.

The Bolshemys culture (4000 to 3000 BC) was a community of foot hunters living in the Altai Mountains of South Siberia, among the Katun, Biya, Irtysh and Ob rivers. The discovery of a metal awl among house remains confirmed that the culture, once classed as Neolithic, actually belonged to the Eneolithic age.

Chemical analysis of pottery from the Botai culture in northern Kazakhstan revealed fatty acid residues from mare's milk, dated to roughly 3500 to 3700 BCE. This is regarded as compelling evidence that Botai people were milking domestic horses this early.

As the Botai culture developed, stone tool making shifted from the tiny microliths used by earlier hunter groups to larger, carefully shaped bifaces. Botai crafters also worked horse bone alongside stone to produce their tools.

Genetic study of Afanasievo individuals showed they were very close to the Yamnaya population of the Pontic–Caspian steppe. They were much more similar to Yamnaya than to groups living between the two regions. This indicates the culture reached the Altai by migration from the western steppe, with little mixing with local peoples.

Archaeologists found wear facets 3 millimetres deep or more on seven horse premolars at the Botai culture sites of Botai and Kozhai 1, dated to about 3700 to 3500 BCE. These are the earliest reported multiple examples of this dental damage, appearing about 1,000 years before any skeletal signs of domestication.

Genetic testing shows that Botai horses were primarily ancestors of today's Przewalski's horse, contributing only about 2.7% of the ancestry of modern domestic horses. This suggests most modern domestic horses descend from horses domesticated somewhere else entirely.

Mesolithic groups who moved into the Kelteminar culture's territory from the Hissar region (6000 to 4000 BCE) brought with them the bow and arrow and the dog. This shift has been described as part of a 'broad-spectrum revolution' by Kent Flannery.

Botai horses were mainly ancestors of Przewalski's horses. They contributed only 2.7% of the ancestry of modern domestic horses. This suggests that modern horses may have been domesticated in other centres of origin.

Even though the Botai lived at the same time as nearby copper-working cultures, no evidence of metalworking has been found at Botai sites. Instead, Botai toolmakers relied on stone and horse bone, shifting from the small microliths of earlier hunting cultures to larger stone bifaces.

Between about 3500 and 3000 BCE, horse bones began turning up more often at sites beyond their main range in the Eurasian steppes, reaching central Europe, the Danube valley, and the North Caucasus and Transcaucasia. Horses may have been deliberately captured and penned, at least for food. This spread happened at the same time as the Botai culture, where there are signs that horses were corralled and ridden.

Genetic analysis of five Botai specimens, four male and one female, found high affinity with Western Siberian hunter-gatherers. The comparison individuals were three hunter-gatherers from Tyumen Oblast, dated to about 5,000 BC. Both groups derive their ancestry mainly from an Ancient North Eurasian-like source.

politics.text: Sarazm, founded in what is now Tajikistan during the first half of the 4th millennium BC, grew into the first city in Central Asia to build lasting economic relations with a wide network of settlements. Its ties stretched from the Turkmenistan steppes and the Aral Sea in the northwest to the Iranian Plateau and the Indus in the south and southeast.

The Kelteminar people, who fished and gathered across the Karakum and Kyzyl Kum deserts between 5500 and 3500 BCE, built huge communal houses up to 24 by 17 meters and 10 meters high. Each house sheltered an entire tribal community of about 100 to 120 people.

The Botai culture of what is now northern Kazakhstan built a settlement with at least 153 pit-houses between about 3700 and 3100 BCE, the largest of its culture's sites. Partly destroyed over time by river erosion, it remains a key example of early permanent settlement on the steppe.

According to archaeologist David W. Anthony, the people of the Afanasievo culture who settled the Altai Mountains and Minusinsk Basin of southern Siberia around 3300 BCE were not descended from earlier local Siberian groups. Instead they arrived as newcomers, having migrated across the Eurasian Steppe from the Repin culture of the Don-Volga region between about 3700 and 3300 BCE.

Around 3500 BC, the farming settlements of southern Turkmenistan split into two distinct groups, marked by different pottery styles: a colorful style in the west at Anau, Kara-Depe and Namazga-Depe, and a plainer style in the east at Altyn-Depe and the Geoksiur Oasis. Archaeologists believe this split may reflect the formation of two separate tribal groups.

Around 3000 BC, people from the Geoksiur Oasis in southern Turkmenistan migrated east into the Murghab delta and further still into the Zerafshan Valley, where they settled at Sarazm near Pendjikent. This movement linked farming communities across Turkmenistan, Afghanistan and Iran into a single, connected network of settlements.

culture.text: The Botai culture flourished c. 3700–3100 BC in what is now northern Kazakhstan. Evidence reported in 2009 included pottery containing mare's milk and horse bones showing signs of breeding. This made a much stronger case that the Botai used domestic horses by about 3,500 BC, close to 1,000 years earlier than scientists had thought.

The Afanasievo culture occupied the Minusinsk Basin and the Altai Mountains of south Siberia, c. 3300 to 2500 BCE. Its people are thought to have migrated across the Eurasian Steppe from the Repin culture of the Don-Volga region. Their burials have been found as far as Shatar Chuluu in central Mongolia, about 1,500 km beyond the Altai Mountains.

Late Mesolithic cultures of Central Asia in the 6th to 5th millennia BC made a distinctive pottery with point or knob bases and flared rims. Their methods were not those used by Neolithic farmers, and farming was absent. The earliest form of this pottery may have appeared around Lake Baikal in Siberia.

The Botai site lies on the Imanburlyq, a tributary of the Ishim, and has at least 153 pit-houses. Part of the settlement has been destroyed by river erosion, which is still going on. Botai gave its name to the whole culture, which also has large sites at Krasnyi Yar and Vasilkovka.

Botai settlements show no evidence of metallurgy, even though other steppe cultures worked metal at the same time. Their tools were made from stone and horse bones. Stone toolmaking shifted from the tiny microliths of earlier nomadic hunter cultures to larger bifaces.
Botai pottery had simple shapes, and most pieces were grey and unglazed. Decoration was geometric, including hatched triangles, rhombi and step motifs. Punctates and circles were also used as motifs.

The Afanasievo culture may show borrowings from the earlier Banpo culture (c. 4000 BCE), especially in painted pottery. This suggests influence from Neolithic China on the Afanasievo and other cultures of the Middle Yenisei region.

The Afanasievo culture is named after Gora Afanasieva, a nearby mountain in Khakassia, Russia. The archaeologist Sergei Teploukhov first excavated there from 1920 to 1929. Radiocarbon dates as early as 3705 BC on wooden tools have now been rejected, leaving about 3300 BC as the start of the culture.

Tamaz Gamkrelidze proposed that the Botai spoke a form of Yeniseian, and Václav Blažek reviewed the idea. Blažek says the linguistic data lend some support to a Yeniseian homeland in the Central Asian Steppe before a migration into Siberia. Such a language could have given words for horsemanship and pastoralism, such as the word for horse, to proto-Indo-European.
